stories.body: At least 254 people have been reported dead after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, with the worst damage in Pereira and Cali. Thousands of homes were damaged and dozens of buildings collapsed. Rescue teams and volunteers are searching rubble for people believed trapped, including at a collapsed residential building in Cali that also fell onto a neighbouring nursery. Authorities have reported thousands injured, hundreds missing or trapped, and continuing aftershocks across the region.
stories.headline: Colombia earthquake death toll rises above 250 as rescuers search for survivors

stories.body: Renewed attacks on commercial shipping have undermined hopes for a swift agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, pushing Brent crude close to $90 a barrel. Yemen's internationally recognised government said Houthi missile attacks killed six people aboard a vessel in the Bab al-Mandab, while US Central Command said it disabled a Panama-flagged cargo ship that attempted to break the US blockade of Iranian ports. Qatar said talks between Oman and Iran were advanced, but Tehran maintained that reopening the strait depends on US concessions including reparations and sanctions relief. Maritime traffic remains far below pre-war levels.
stories.headline: Attacks on shipping deepen impasse over Strait of Hormuz talks

stories.body: North Korea launched a ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the Sea of Japan, according to South Korean and Japanese authorities, in its second such test in less than a week. South Korea said the missile travelled more than 700 kilometres and that it had strengthened surveillance while sharing information with Washington and Tokyo. The launch came as Seoul and Washington announced that their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises would begin on August 17, involving about 18,000 South Korean troops. Pyongyang has historically denounced the drills as invasion rehearsals and often responds with weapons tests.
stories.headline: North Korea launches another ballistic missile before US-South Korea drills

stories.body: Russia and Ukraine carried out overnight strikes as Ukrainian officials said attacks on Zaporizhzhia killed at least seven workers at a steel plant and involved North Korean ballistic missiles. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia could no longer sustain its war without reinforcements from North Korea, though he did not publicly provide evidence for the latest claim. Russian strikes also damaged buildings in Kyiv and hit Sumy, while Ukraine struck warehouses in Voronezh and a petrochemical facility in western Siberia. The exchanges followed Ukrainian drone attacks that reportedly killed at least 13 people in Russia's Tatarstan region.
stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine exchange major strikes as Kyiv says Moscow used North Korean missiles

stories.body: Wisconsin Democrats were left without a clear result in their closely watched gubernatorial primary, a contest seen as a test of the party's debate between progressive and more moderate approaches. The race between Francesca Hong and David Crowley remained too close to call, while primary outcomes elsewhere in the Midwest also highlighted competing factions within the Democratic Party. The inconclusive Wisconsin result offered little immediate indication of which direction Democratic voters may favour ahead of the general election.
stories.headline: Wisconsin Democratic governor primary remains too close to call

stories.body: Progressive candidates scored important wins in Minnesota Democratic primaries, according to Associated Press reporting on Tuesday's elections. The results, alongside the unresolved Wisconsin governor's primary, underscored continuing disagreements within the party over whether to embrace more progressive candidates or centrist alternatives. The contests are being closely watched for what they may indicate about Democratic electoral strategy ahead of November.
stories.headline: Minnesota progressives win key Democratic primaries

stories.body: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to spend up to $20 million on thousands of gloves designed to deliver a painful electrical shock when applied to a person's skin, according to a Department of Homeland Security notice. The devices, known as G.L.O.V.E. units, are intended to gain compliance from combative individuals and function as ordinary patrol gloves until activated. Civil-rights advocates warned that ICE already faces concerns over oversight and use of force, while the manufacturer says the gloves should not be used as punishment or on children, pregnant people, elderly people, or people with disabilities.
stories.headline: ICE plans to equip officers with gloves capable of delivering electric shocks

stories.body: Severe thunderstorms and tornadoes cut power to more than half a million people in the Chicago area and northwestern Indiana, causing widespread damage as storms swept across the Midwest. Homes in suburbs including Tinley Park were damaged, while lightning injured people at an Ohio prison. The outbreak was linked to a summer weather pattern often described as a 'ring of fire,' which can bring repeated severe storms around the edge of a heat dome.
stories.headline: Severe Midwest storms knock out power across Illinois, Indiana and Ohio

stories.body: Spain is preparing for its first total solar eclipse in more than a century, with the Moon's shadow expected to cross the country from Galicia to the Balearic Islands on Wednesday evening. Totality will last roughly one to two minutes, with the maximum in Spain expected around 8:30pm local time. Authorities have warned of heavy traffic, especially on routes toward observation areas in Tarragona and the Ebro Delta, and urged people not to stop on roads or shoulders. Officials are also concerned about cloud cover in some northern areas, last-minute travel and a high to extreme wildfire risk across much of the country.
stories.headline: Spain prepares for total solar eclipse amid travel, weather and safety concerns

stories.body: Spain's government and the opposition People's Party agree that family reunification in Morocco should be the priority for the 1,527 unaccompanied minors identified after the mass arrival in Ceuta. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said Spain and Morocco were committed to the return of people who entered irregularly, but the proposed returns face significant legal constraints. Spanish law requires individual assessments, information about each child's family circumstances, hearings for sufficiently mature minors, and involvement by child-protection services and prosecutors. Spain's Supreme Court ruled that group returns of minors from Ceuta in 2021 were unlawful.
stories.headline: Spanish government and opposition agree unaccompanied minors in Ceuta should return to Morocco

stories.body: Spain's government says ministers will answer to the Senate over the Ceuta migration crisis, but not on the timetable demanded by the opposition-controlled upper chamber. The People's Party had sought urgent appearances by the defence, interior and foreign ministers after thousands of people entered Ceuta irregularly in late July. Defence Minister Margarita Robles may appear on August 18, but Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska and Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares have said they will instead give accounts in Congress later in August. Parliamentary experts say the government must respond to requests to appear, although the law provides no sanction or fixed date if it does not comply immediately.
stories.headline: Spanish government and Senate clash over ministers' appearances on Ceuta migration crisis

stories.body: The wildfire near Niebla in Huelva remains active after burning more than 25,000 hectares of eucalyptus plantations, pastureland, scrub and pine forest, according to a provisional regional estimate. About 700 people remain evacuated from several municipalities. Andalusian authorities said some fronts were contained overnight but warned that the large perimeter would require days of work to secure and prevent flare-ups. More than 500 personnel from the Military Emergency Unit and Civil Guard are involved, while strong winds, convective conditions and spot fires several kilometres from the main blaze have complicated containment efforts.
stories.headline: Niebla wildfire remains active after burning more than 25,000 hectares

stories.body: Catalan authorities have activated a special operation for the total solar eclipse, anticipating heavy travel toward Tarragona, Lleida and the Ebro region, where the phenomenon will be total. The Catalan Traffic Service has urged visitors to stagger journeys and avoid the AP-7 where possible, warning of likely congestion on the two-lane stretch between Cambrils and Ulldecona. In Barcelona, where about 99.7% of the Sun will be obscured, the Guàrdia Urbana will deploy operational units from 2pm until midnight, with heightened attention to Collserola, Montjuïc and routes into and out of the city. The measures are intended to prevent crowding, illegal parking, restricted-area access and opportunistic theft.
stories.headline: Barcelona and Catalonia put special traffic and safety measures in place for the eclipse

stories.body: Car-rental firms in Barcelona are struggling to meet demand during eclipse week, with prices rising from typical rates of about €100 a day to €800 or more, and in some cases more than €1,300 for two days. One company said it added around 50 vehicles to its fleet but still lacked supply. Local customers are largely travelling south toward Tarragona, while many foreign visitors are heading toward Zaragoza. Rental staff said many foreign tourists booked months in advance, whereas local customers made more last-minute reservations, and availability is expected to remain tight through the August holiday period.
stories.headline: Eclipse demand leaves Barcelona car-rental companies short of vehicles and drives up prices

stories.body: A marine heatwave has pushed sea-surface temperatures above 30C in parts of the Catalan coast and the Balearic Islands. A buoy off Barcelona recorded 30.5C, around 3C above the recent seasonal average, while Tarragona reached 30.7C. Near Sa Dragonera in Mallorca, a buoy recorded 33.02C. The western and central Mediterranean are experiencing widespread anomalies of roughly 3C to 5C, with potentially serious consequences for marine biodiversity and added atmospheric moisture that can intensify heavy rainfall when other conditions are present. Researchers also warn that rising Mediterranean temperatures will contribute to more frequent and intense urban heatwaves in coming decades.
stories.headline: Mediterranean marine heatwave pushes sea temperatures above 30C off Catalonia and the Balearics

stories.body: Barcelona will install 99 new security cameras before the end of the year as part of a wider plan that aims to expand the city's network from 186 current devices to about 660 by 2027. The next installations include cameras at the Born promenade, the Carmel bunkers, the Olympic Ring, the Encants Vells and Fort Pienc area, and Pegaso Park. The city says the cameras will support crime prevention, incident response and evidence gathering in places with high footfall or documented security and coexistence concerns. Officials say the system will not use facial recognition or other artificial-intelligence-based identification technologies, and recordings remain subject to data-protection rules and regional authorization.
stories.headline: Barcelona to install around 100 new security cameras before year-end
